what_its_for: This device delivers insulin just under your skin (subcutaneously) to help control your blood sugar levels. Insulin helps your body use sugar from food for energy and keeps your blood sugar from getting too high. It is used to manage Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes.
how_to_take: 1. Wash your hands with soap and water before starting. 2. Check the insulin in your device — it should look clear or evenly cloudy (depending on your insulin type). Do not use if it looks discolored, has clumps, or particles. 3. Attach a new needle by twisting it onto the pen tip until snug. 4. Prime the pen: Dial 2 units, point the pen up, and press the button until you see a drop of insulin at the needle tip. This removes air bubbles. 5. Dial your prescribed dose on the dose window — you can set up to 30 units with this device. 6. Choose your injection site: belly (at least 2 inches from the belly button), outer thigh, upper arm, or buttocks. Rotate sites each time to avoid skin changes. 7. Pinch a fold of skin gently, insert the needle at a 90-degree angle (or 45 degrees if you are thin), and press the injection button all the way down. 8. Hold the needle in place for 10 seconds after injecting so all the insulin is delivered. 9. Remove the needle and dispose of it safely in a sharps container. Never reuse needles. 10. Replace the pen cap when done.
dosing: Your doctor will prescribe a specific dose for you based on your blood sugar levels, diet, and activity. This device holds up to 30 units per injection. Take your insulin exactly as prescribed — at the same time each day or with meals, depending on your insulin type. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor or diabetes care team first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, check your blood sugar right away. For fast-acting (mealtime) insulin: if it is still close to mealtime, take it as soon as possible. If your next meal is very soon or you have already eaten, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. For long-acting (basal) insulin: take it as soon as you remember the same day. If it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed one. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. Call your doctor or diabetes team if you are unsure what to do.
storage: Unopened insulin pens: Store in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze insulin — throw it away if it has been frozen. In-use (opened) insulin pens: Most can be stored at room temperature (below 77°F or 25°C) for 28 to 56 days depending on your specific insulin brand. Check your insulin package insert for exact timeframes. Keep the pen cap on when not in use. Store away from direct sunlight and heat (do not leave in a hot car). Always check the expiration date before using.
what_to_avoid: Avoid injecting into the same spot repeatedly — this can cause lumpy or hardened skin that makes insulin work poorly. Avoid alcohol swabbing the injection site right before injecting, as this can sting and may affect absorption. Avoid sharing your insulin pen or needles with anyone else, even family members, due to serious infection risks. Avoid skipping meals after taking mealtime insulin, as this can cause dangerously low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol, as it can cause unpredictable blood sugar changes. Avoid exposing your insulin device to extreme temperatures, direct sunlight, or vigorous shaking.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help right away if you have: signs of very low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) such as shaking, sweating, dizziness, confusion, fast heartbeat, or passing out; signs of very high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) such as extreme thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, or fruity-smelling breath; signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing, or rapid heartbeat; redness, swelling, pain, or skin changes at your injection site that do not go away; unusual weight gain or swelling in your hands or feet; repeated blood sugar readings outside your target range; illness, infection, or surgery that may affect your blood sugar control.
when_it_works: The time it takes for insulin to work depends on the type you are using. Fast-acting insulin (like Humalog or Novolog) starts working within 15 minutes, peaks in 1 to 2 hours, and lasts 3 to 5 hours. Long-acting insulin (like Lantus or Tresiba) starts working within 1 to 2 hours and provides steady blood sugar control for 24 hours or longer. Your blood sugar control typically improves within days to weeks of starting insulin therapy, but your doctor will monitor your A1C (a 3-month blood sugar average) to track how well your treatment is working over time.
special_populations: Older adults (65+): You may be more sensitive to insulin and at higher risk for low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Your doctor may start you on a lower dose and monitor you more closely. Children and teenagers: Dosing is carefully adjusted based on weight and growth. Always have a parent or caregiver involved in insulin administration for young children. Pregnant women: Insulin needs often change during pregnancy. Work closely with your doctor and diabetes care team to adjust doses safely. Kidney or liver disease: These conditions can affect how long insulin stays in your body and may increase your risk of low blood sugar. More frequent monitoring and possible dose adjustments may be needed. People with vision problems or limited hand strength: Ask your pharmacist or doctor about magnifying aids or devices designed to help with insulin pen use.
